what: Schneider National hauls freight. It owns thousands of trucks and employs drivers to carry truckload freight, runs intermodal services moving containers by rail and truck together, and arranges freight for others as a broker without using its own equipment.
customers: Manufacturers, retailers and food companies shipping goods across North America, from large national accounts to smaller shippers using its brokerage.
money: Freight hauled by its own trucks and drivers, including dedicated fleets for specific customers.
Containers moved by rail for the long haul and truck at each end.
Freight arranged for customers using other carriers’ trucks.
moat: Dedicated fleets — trucks and drivers assigned to one customer’s freight under a multi-year contract — are the best part of trucking: the revenue is contracted rather than spot-priced, and the customer is committed. Intermodal is structurally cheaper than trucking over long distances, because a train moves freight at a fraction of the fuel cost per mile.
risks: Reported net income of $141.7M gives a price/earnings ratio of 35.2, which reflects earnings at the bottom of the freight cycle.
Last year’s net margin was 1.8%, the structural reality of asset-based trucking: the trucks cost the same whether loaded or not.
Revenue fell from $6.6B in 2022 to $5.3B in 2024 as freight rates collapsed from pandemic highs.
Owning the trucks means fixed costs that do not fall when volumes do, unlike an asset-light broker.
Fourteen analysts average a $35.00 target, about 23% above the current price.
opportunities: Debt of $492.3M against $243.3M of cash is conservative for a company with a large truck fleet.
The shares trade at about 7.8 times EV/EBITDA and 0.84 times sales, modest multiples at a cyclical trough.
Dedicated contract fleets provide revenue that is contracted rather than exposed to the spot market.
Intermodal is structurally cheaper than long-haul trucking, and that cost advantage grows when diesel is expensive.
Free cash flow of $258.4M even at the bottom of the cycle shows the business is not in distress.
watch: Revenue per truck per week, and the dedicated share of the truckload fleet. The dedicated business is the quality part; spot freight is the cycle.
view: Asset-based trucking is a hard business and the arithmetic explains why: the truck costs the same, the driver is paid the same, and the insurance is the same whether the trailer is full or empty. A 1.8% net margin is not mismanagement; it is the structure. When freight demand collapses — revenue fell from $6.6 billion to $5.3 billion — those fixed costs eat the earnings, which is exactly what has happened.

Within that, Schneider has deliberately shifted toward the better parts. Dedicated fleets, where trucks and drivers are assigned to one customer’s freight under a multi-year contract, are the best thing in trucking: the rate is contracted rather than set by a spot market that moves weekly, and the customer is committed. The more of the fleet that is dedicated, the less the earnings swing.

Intermodal is the other structurally sound piece and it is often misunderstood. Moving a container by rail for the long haul and truck at each end is substantially cheaper per mile than trucking the whole way, because a train burns a fraction of the fuel. That advantage widens when diesel is expensive and narrows when it is cheap, but it does not go away — it is physics rather than strategy.

The reported 35.2 times price/earnings ratio is a trough multiple, not an expensive stock, and the same operating leverage works powerfully in reverse when freight recovers. What makes the wait tolerable is the balance sheet: $492 million of debt against $243 million of cash is genuinely conservative for a fleet operator, which means Schneider can survive a long freight recession that forces weaker carriers to sell trucks. Revenue per truck per week and the dedicated share of the fleet are the two numbers worth following.
bull: Freight rates recover against a conservative balance sheet while the dedicated and intermodal mix reduces earnings volatility, lifting trough earnings sharply.
bear: The freight recession drags on for years, fixed fleet costs keep margins near 2%, and operating leverage works against the earnings throughout.
